summary: Describes a backward-compatible technique for OSPF to exchange arbitrary data between neighbors on a link, called link-local signaling. OSPF packet formats were too rigid for new features, so this adds an extensible block.

eli5.summary: OSPF packets had no spare room for extra notes. This adds a small pocket on the envelope that old readers ignore but new readers can use.

questions: what is the ospf lls block
which ospf packets can carry lls data
subtitle: A backward-compatible way to tack extra data onto OSPF Hello and Database Description packets.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 packet formats are fixed and cannot carry new kinds of data between neighbouring routers.
tldr.mechanism: A router appends an optional block of Type/Length/Value triplets (the LLS block) to Hello and Database Description packets and sets the new L-bit in the Options field to say it is there.
tldr.outcome: Routers that do not understand LLS ignore the extra block, so new features can be signalled on a link without breaking old routers. This document moves the idea from RFC 4813 (Experimental) to the Standards Track.

facts.label: Carried by
facts.value: Hello and Database Description packets only

today: RFC 5613 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 4813, adding OSPFv3 support and requiring private TLVs to use a private enterprise code. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why OSPF Needs Link-Local Signaling
sections.content:
OSPF routers on the same link talk using packets with a fixed, well-defined format. RFC 2328 (OSPFv2) and RFC 5340 (OSPFv3) leave no room in those formats for new kinds of data. Link-local signaling (LLS) is the fix: an optional block of data appended to existing OSPF packets, made of Type/Length/Value (TLV) triplets.

The RFC considers and sets aside the obvious alternative, a brand new packet type. That would add extra packets to the network and could cause backward compatibility problems. Reusing the standard packet types avoids both.
sections.eli5: The old OSPF letters had no space for a postscript. This idea lets a router staple a small extra page to the letter that only newer routers read.

sections.title: Attaching the LLS Block
sections.content:
A router adds the LLS block to the end of an OSPF packet, or right after the authentication data when cryptographic authentication is used. The block's length is not counted in the OSPF packet length, but it is counted in the IPv4 or IPv6 packet length.

The block MAY be attached to Hello and Database Description (DD) packets only. It MUST NOT be attached to any other OSPF packet type, and it must be ignored if received on one.

The two carriers behave differently. Data in a Hello can be sent at any time, so it suits dynamic signaling, but its delivery is not guaranteed. Data in DD packets is guaranteed to arrive as part of forming an adjacency.

The RFC does not say how routers should interpret LLS data. Because routers without LLS support just ignore the block, changes driven by LLS TLVs do not affect basic routing when talking to such routers.
sections.eli5: The extra page goes only on two kinds of letters, the hello letters and the introduction letters. Hello letters can be sent any time but might get lost. Introduction letters always get through.

sections.title: The L-bit and the LLS Block Format
sections.content:
A new L-bit in the OSPF Options field tells a receiver that the packet carries an LLS block. The block is only examined if the L-bit is set, and the L-bit MUST NOT be set except in Hello and DD packets that actually contain an LLS block.

The block starts with a 16-bit Checksum and a 16-bit LLS Data Length, followed by the TLVs. The checksum is the standard IP checksum over the whole block, computed with the checksum field set to 0. If it is wrong, the OSPF packet is still processed but the LLS block is discarded. The length is counted in 32-bit words and includes the header.

If the OSPF packet is cryptographically authenticated, the LLS block must be authenticated too. In that case the regular checksum is not calculated and is set to 0.
sections.eli5: A little flag on the envelope says there is an extra page inside. The extra page begins with a quick check number and a note saying how long it is.

sections.title: TLVs and the Two Defined Types
sections.content:
Each TLV has a 16-bit Type, a 16-bit Length (the length of the Value in bytes) and a variable Value. TLVs are padded to a 32-bit boundary. The padding is not counted in the TLV Length but is counted in the LLS Data Length. Unrecognized TLV types are ignored.

The Extended Options and Flags (EOF) TLV has type 1 and a 4-byte Value. Its bits have no meaning to the LLS mechanism itself; they may be allocated to announce link-local capabilities or to do boolean signaling. It MUST appear only once in the block. The RFC notes that the out-of-band LSDB resynchronization (RFC 4811) and restart signaling (RFC 4812) specifications use bits in it.

Type values 32768 to 65535 are for private use. The first four octets of the Value of a private TLV MUST be the private enterprise code, so several vendors' extensions can coexist in one network.
sections.eli5: The extra page is a list of small labelled notes. Each note says what kind it is, how long it is, and then gives the message. A router just skips notes it does not know.

sections.title: Cryptographic Authentication TLV
sections.content:
For OSPFv2 only, type 2 defines the CA-TLV, used when cryptographic authentication is enabled on the interface. The message digest of the LLS block is computed with the same key and algorithm as the OSPFv2 packet.

The TLV carries a cryptographic sequence number that prevents simple replay attacks. It MUST match the sequence number in the OSPFv2 packet header Authentication field, or the whole LLS block MUST be ignored. The same applies if authentication fails.

The CA-TLV must not appear more than once and, when present, must be the last TLV. The digest covers the LLS block up to, but not including, the AuthData field. It does not apply to OSPFv3 and MUST NOT be added to OSPFv3 packets; if found, it is ignored.
sections.eli5: To prove the extra page was not tampered with, the router signs it with the same secret stamp it uses on the letter, and writes down the letter's serial number so the two can be matched.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Allocation Rules
sections.content:
The document reuses the LLS TLV registry created by RFC 4813 and points it at this RFC. IANA also allocated the L-bit in the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 Options registries. TLV type 0 is reserved, 1 is the Extended Options and Flags TLV, 2 is the Cryptographic Authentication TLV, 3 to 32767 are reserved for IANA assignment, and 32768 to 65535 are private use.

Types 0 to 32767 are allocated through IETF Review, and new TLV types and new EOF bits must be reviewed by a Designated Expert from the routing area. Two EOF bits are assigned: 0x00000001 for LSDB Resynchronization (LR) and 0x00000002 for the Restart Signal (RS-bit).

The allocation criteria are advice to future authors. LLS should not carry information better advertised in a link-local LSA, should stay between direct neighbours, and should be used sparingly because of MTU and performance implications.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of note types so that nobody reuses the same number for different things. A few numbers are saved for companies to use privately.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
The change is compatible with standard OSPF because routers that do not support LLS ignore the data after the OSPF packet or after the cryptographic message digest. The RFC notes implementations were already deployed with software compliant with RFC 4813. It also warns that extra LLS data can lengthen OSPF adjacency bring-up because of added propagation or processing time.

On security, LLS gives the same level of protection as basic OSPFv2, since its data can use the same cryptographic authentication. For OSPFv3, IPsec AH, ESP or both are applied to the whole OSPFv3 payload including the LLS block.
sections.eli5: Old routers simply do not look at the extra page, so nothing breaks. The extra page is protected the same way as the letter it rides on.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard IP checksum over the whole LLS block, computed with this field set to 0.

fields.name: LLS Data Length
fields.desc: Length of the block including header and payload, in 32-bit words.

items.label: Extended Options and Flags
items.desc: 4-byte Value of capability and signaling bits.

items.label: Cryptographic Authentication
items.desc: OSPFv2 only; carries sequence number and digest.

items.label: Private Use
items.desc: Value starts with a private enterprise code.
